title.en: Section 1 - Registering for a Fitness Programme
title.zh: 第一部分 - 注册健身计划

sections.passage: A conversation between a new member, Sarah, and a receptionist at a fitness centre called FitLife. Sarah has recently moved to the area and wants to join a gym. The receptionist, Marcus, explains the membership options. FitLife offers three plans: a Pay-As-You-Go plan at 8 pounds per visit, a Monthly Unlimited plan at 55 pounds per month with a minimum three-month commitment, and an Annual Membership at 499 pounds per year, which works out to approximately 42 pounds per month. Marcus mentions that the Annual Membership also includes two free personal training sessions, a complimentary fitness assessment, and a 15 percent discount at the on-site juice bar. Sarah is interested in the Monthly Unlimited plan because she is not sure how long she will be staying in the area. Marcus asks about her fitness goals, and Sarah explains that she wants to improve her cardiovascular fitness and lose some weight. He recommends that she try the group exercise classes, particularly the spinning classes on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday mornings at 7 AM, and the HIIT classes on Tuesday and Thursday evenings at 6:30 PM. Sarah asks about the swimming pool, and Marcus tells her it is a twenty-metre pool open from 6 AM to 9 PM on weekdays and 8 AM to 6 PM on weekends. He also mentions that the centre has a sauna and steam room, which are available to all members at no extra charge. Sarah decides to sign up for the Monthly Unlimited plan and fills in the registration form. Marcus gives her a membership card and a free gym towel as a welcome gift. He tells her that the first payment will be taken on the 1st of next month and that she can freeze her membership for up to one month per year if needed.

title.en: Section 2 - Introduction to a Recycling Programme
title.zh: 第二部分 - 回收计划介绍

sections.passage: Good evening, and thank you for coming to tonight's community meeting. My name is Peter Lawson, and I'm the Environmental Services coordinator for Greenfield Borough Council. I'm here to introduce our new comprehensive recycling programme, which will begin on the 1st of April. The council has invested 1.5 million pounds in new recycling infrastructure, including a state-of-the-art materials recovery facility on Industrial Way and a fleet of twelve new collection vehicles. Under the new system, residents will sort their recyclable waste into four categories. The blue bin is for paper and cardboard, including newspapers, magazines, office paper, cereal boxes, and cardboard packaging. However, we cannot accept paper that has been contaminated with food, such as used pizza boxes or paper towels. The green bin is for glass bottles and jars of any colour, as well as metal cans, tin foil, and aerosol cans. Please rinse all containers before placing them in the bin. The red bin is for plastic bottles, pots, tubs, and trays marked with recycling symbols one through five. We cannot currently accept plastic bags, cling film, or polystyrene packaging, though we hope to expand the programme in the future. Finally, the brown bin is for garden waste, including grass cuttings, hedge trimmings, and small branches, but not soil, stones, or food waste. Collection days will vary depending on your street. Residents on streets beginning with letters A through F will have collection on Mondays, G through L on Tuesdays, M through R on Wednesdays, and S through Z on Thursdays. All bins should be placed at the kerbside by 7 AM on your collection day. Any waste that does not fit into these categories should go into your existing black general waste bin. I should emphasise that contaminated recycling — that is, recyclable materials mixed with non-recyclable waste — cannot be processed and will be sent to landfill, so it is very important that residents sort their waste correctly. For those who are unsure about which items go in which bin, we have produced a comprehensive guide that will be delivered to every household, and there is also a searchable database on the council's website. Additionally, we are recruiting volunteer recycling ambassadors who will be available to answer questions at community events and shopping centres.

title.en: Section 3 - Students Discussing a Science Experiment
title.zh: 第三部分 - 学生讨论科学实验

sections.passage: Two undergraduate students, Tom and Aisha, are discussing their upcoming laboratory experiment for their Biology module. They need to investigate the effect of different light wavelengths on the rate of photosynthesis in aquatic plants. Their professor, Dr. Patel, has provided a detailed protocol, and they are reviewing the materials and methodology. Tom has prepared a list of required materials: a water plant called Elodea canadensis, a beaker, a light source with interchangeable colour filters — red, blue, green, and white — a ruler, a stopwatch, and a thermometer. The experiment involves counting the number of oxygen bubbles produced by the plant under each light colour as an indicator of the photosynthesis rate. Aisha raises a concern about controlling variables. She points out that the distance between the light source and the plant must remain constant at thirty centimetres throughout all trials to ensure a fair test. Tom agrees and adds that the water temperature should also be monitored and kept at approximately 20 degrees Celsius, since temperature affects the rate of photosynthesis. They plan to conduct five trials for each light colour to ensure reliable results and calculate the mean number of bubbles per minute. Aisha suggests running the experiment in a darkened room to prevent ambient light from affecting the results. Tom proposes starting with the white light as a baseline, then testing red, blue, and green in sequence. They predict that blue light will produce the highest rate of photosynthesis, followed by red, with green producing the lowest rate because chlorophyll absorbs blue and red light most efficiently while reflecting green light. They agree to write up the results as a formal lab report, which should include a title, aim, hypothesis, method, results table with mean calculations, a bar chart showing the results, a discussion of their findings in relation to their hypothesis, and a conclusion. The report is due on the 15th of November and should be approximately 2,000 words. They plan to conduct the experiment on Wednesday afternoon and write up the report together over the weekend.

title.zh: 第四部分 - 关于城市野生动物的讲座

sections.passage:
Good morning. Today's lecture examines the fascinating and often overlooked subject of urban wildlife — the animals and plants that have adapted to live alongside humans in cities and towns. As urbanisation continues to accelerate globally, with the United Nations predicting that 68 percent of the world's population will live in urban areas by 2050, understanding how wildlife adapts to urban environments has become increasingly important for both conservation biology and urban planning.

Many species have demonstrated remarkable adaptability to urban life. The peregrine falcon, once endangered due to pesticide contamination, has made a dramatic comeback by nesting on tall buildings, bridges, and church steeples that mimic the cliff faces of its natural habitat. Urban peregrine populations are now thriving in cities across Europe and North America, with some pairs successfully raising chicks on skyscrapers in city centres. Similarly, red foxes have become ubiquitous in British cities, with an estimated population of 150,000 urban foxes in the UK. Research by the University of Bristol has shown that urban foxes have developed different behaviours compared to their rural counterparts, including smaller home ranges, altered feeding habits, and greater tolerance of human proximity.

However, urbanisation also creates significant challenges for wildlife. Habitat fragmentation is perhaps the most critical issue. As cities expand, natural habitats are broken into smaller, isolated patches that may be too small to support viable populations of many species. Roads present a particular threat, with an estimated one million vertebrates killed on roads in the UK every day. Light pollution disrupts the behaviour of nocturnal species, affecting feeding patterns, migration, and reproduction. Noise pollution can interfere with bird song, reducing breeding success in species that rely on vocal communication to attract mates. A study in the Netherlands found that great tits in noisy urban areas sang at higher frequencies than their rural counterparts to be heard above the traffic.

Despite these challenges, cities can support surprisingly high levels of biodiversity when appropriate management strategies are employed. Urban green spaces — including parks, gardens, allotments, cemeteries, and brownfield sites — serve as crucial refugia for wildlife. Research in Sheffield, England, found that domestic gardens collectively covered a larger area than all the city's parks and nature reserves combined, making them vital habitats for species such as hedgehogs, songbirds, and pollinating insects. Green corridors — connected strips of habitat that allow wildlife to move between larger green spaces — are increasingly being incorporated into urban planning to combat the effects of fragmentation. The London National Park City initiative, launched in 2019, aims to make London the world's first National Park City, with ambitious targets for increasing green cover and connecting wildlife habitats across the capital.

Some urban species have even thrived to the point of becoming management challenges. Canada geese, introduced to the UK from North America, have proliferated in urban parks and waterways, causing problems through aggressive behaviour, noise, and the fouling of public spaces with droppings. Mute swans, ring-necked parakeets, and grey squirrels are other examples of species that have adapted so successfully to urban life that they sometimes come into conflict with human residents. Managing these human-wildlife conflicts requires a nuanced approach that balances the ecological value of urban wildlife with the legitimate concerns of residents. The most effective strategies typically involve habitat management, public education, and, where necessary, humane population control measures, rather than outright eradication. Ultimately, the goal should be to create cities that are not just habitable for humans but that also provide space for the remarkable diversity of life that can coexist with us when given the opportunity.

sections.passage:
The measurement of time has been a fundamental human concern since the earliest civilizations. The ability to track the passage of hours, days, and seasons was essential for agricultural societies that depended on knowing when to plant and harvest crops, and for navigators who relied on astronomical observations to determine their position at sea. The history of timekeeping is a story of ever-increasing precision, from the observation of celestial bodies to the atomic clocks that underpin modern technology.

The earliest timekeeping devices were sundials, which have been found in archaeological sites dating back to approximately 3500 BC in Egypt and Babylon. A sundial works by casting a shadow from a central gnomon onto a calibrated dial face, allowing the user to read the approximate time based on the shadow's position. While effective during daylight hours in clear weather, sundials were obviously limited at night and on cloudy days. Water clocks, or clepsydrae, were developed as an alternative, with the earliest known examples dating from around 1500 BC in Egypt. These devices measured time by the regulated flow of water from one vessel to another. The Greeks and Romans improved upon the design, and water clocks were widely used in courts of law to time speeches and in military settings to coordinate night watches.

Mechanical clocks emerged in Europe during the 13th century, representing a revolutionary advancement in timekeeping technology. The earliest mechanical clocks used a verge escapement mechanism with a foliot balance, which regulated the release of energy from a falling weight. These clocks were large, heavy, and inaccurate by modern standards — typically losing or gaining 15 to 30 minutes per day — but they transformed European society by enabling the coordination of activities in monasteries, towns, and trading centres. The first public clock tower is believed to have been installed in the cathedral of Dunblane, Scotland, around 1340. By the 15th century, clock-making had become a skilled craft, and domestic clocks began appearing in the homes of the wealthy.

The invention of the pendulum clock by Christiaan Huygens in 1656 was a breakthrough that dramatically improved accuracy. By using the regular swinging motion of a pendulum to regulate the clock mechanism, Huygens achieved an accuracy of about 15 seconds per day, a tenfold improvement over earlier mechanical clocks. Subsequent refinements by clockmakers such as George Graham and Thomas Mudge further improved precision and introduced innovations including the deadbeat escapement and the lever escapement that would dominate clockmaking for centuries.

The quest for accurate timekeeping at sea was driven by the practical need for navigators to determine longitude. In 1714, the British government offered a prize of 20,000 pounds — equivalent to several million pounds today — for a method of determining longitude at sea to within half a degree. John Harrison, a self-taught Yorkshire carpenter and clockmaker, spent decades developing a series of marine chronometers that could keep accurate time despite the motion of a ship and variations in temperature and humidity. His fourth timekeeper, known as H4, completed a transatlantic voyage in 1761 with an error of only five seconds over 81 days, definitively solving the longitude problem. Harrison's achievement was one of the most important technological accomplishments of the 18th century, enabling the age of global maritime exploration and trade.

The 20th century saw the development of quartz crystal oscillators and then atomic clocks, which revolutionised timekeeping. The first atomic clock, built in 1955 at the National Physical Laboratory in England, used the natural vibration frequency of caesium-133 atoms to achieve an accuracy of one second in 300 years. Modern atomic clocks are accurate to one second in approximately 300 million years and form the basis of the Global Positioning System, telecommunications networks, and the internet. The definition of the second itself is now based on atomic time rather than astronomical observations, marking a fundamental shift in humanity's relationship with time.

sections.passage:
For much of the 20th century, the primary measure of a nation's progress was its Gross Domestic Product — the total monetary value of all goods and services produced within a country's borders. However, a growing body of research in economics, psychology, and neuroscience has challenged the assumption that economic growth automatically translates into improved human wellbeing. The field of happiness economics, which studies the relationship between income, policy, and subjective wellbeing, has emerged as a significant area of inquiry that is reshaping how governments think about the goals of public policy.

The pioneering work in this field was conducted by American economist Richard Easterlin, who in 1974 published a landmark paper showing that while richer people within a country tend to report higher levels of happiness than poorer people, increases in national income over time do not correspond to increases in average happiness levels. This finding, known as the Easterlin Paradox, suggested that above a certain threshold of income, additional wealth provides diminishing returns in terms of happiness. Easterlin's work stimulated decades of research and debate, with some economists questioning his methodology while others sought to explain and extend his findings.

More recent research using large international datasets, including the Gallup World Poll and the World Happiness Report, has provided a more nuanced picture. Studies consistently show that while there is a positive correlation between income and happiness, this relationship weakens significantly once a country reaches a moderate level of economic development. The point at which additional income ceases to improve average happiness has been estimated at approximately 75,000 dollars per year in the United States, though this figure varies by country and cost of living. Beyond this threshold, factors such as social connections, health, personal freedom, and work-life balance become much stronger predictors of happiness than income.

The data reveal striking differences in happiness levels across countries that are not fully explained by income alone. Nordic countries — Finland, Denmark, Norway, Sweden, and Iceland — consistently rank among the happiest in the world, despite not being the wealthiest. Researchers attribute this to several factors: strong social safety nets, low levels of corruption, high levels of trust between citizens, excellent public services including healthcare and education, and a cultural emphasis on work-life balance. Finland has topped the World Happiness Report for six consecutive years, and Finnish researchers point to what they call sisu — a cultural concept encompassing resilience, determination, and stoic perseverance — as a contributing factor.

Conversely, some relatively wealthy countries score lower than expected on happiness measures. The United States, despite having one of the highest GDPs per capita, ranks only around 15th to 20th in global happiness surveys. Researchers have pointed to factors including high levels of income inequality, inadequate social safety nets, expensive healthcare, long working hours, and declining social capital as possible explanations. The concept of social capital — the networks of relationships, trust, and norms that enable communities to function effectively — has been identified as a particularly important determinant of happiness. Robert Putnam's influential book Bowling Alone documented the decline of social organisations and community engagement in the United States since the 1960s, arguing that this erosion of social capital has had profound negative effects on both individual wellbeing and democratic participation.

Several countries have begun incorporating happiness and wellbeing metrics into their policy frameworks. Bhutan famously adopted Gross National Happiness as an alternative to GDP in the 1970s, measuring progress across nine domains including psychological wellbeing, health, education, and ecological diversity. New Zealand introduced a Wellbeing Budget in 2019, prioritising mental health, child poverty reduction, and support for Maori and Pacific Islander communities. Scotland, Iceland, and Wales have formed the Wellbeing Economy Governments partnership, committing to designing economic policy around the wellbeing of people and the planet. While the practical implementation of happiness-based policy remains challenging and contested, these experiments represent a significant shift in how societies define and pursue progress.

title.zh: 文章3 - 微生物组革命

sections.passage:
Over the past two decades, a revolution in biological science has fundamentally changed our understanding of the human body and its relationship with the microbial world. The Human Microbiome Project, launched in 2007 by the National Institutes of Health, set out to catalogue the vast community of microorganisms — bacteria, viruses, fungi, and other microbes — that inhabit the human body. The results have been staggering: the average human body contains approximately 38 trillion microbial cells, slightly more than the 30 trillion human cells that make up the body itself. Far from being passive hitchhikers or harmful invaders, these microorganisms play essential roles in digestion, immune function, mental health, and resistance to disease.

The gut microbiome — the community of microbes residing in the digestive tract — has attracted the most scientific attention. The human gut harbours over 1,000 different species of bacteria, collectively weighing approximately two kilograms. These bacteria perform numerous functions that the human body cannot accomplish on its own. They break down complex carbohydrates and dietary fibres that human enzymes cannot digest, producing short-chain fatty acids that nourish the cells lining the colon and regulate inflammation. They synthesise essential vitamins, including vitamin K and several B vitamins. They train and regulate the immune system, teaching it to distinguish between harmful pathogens and harmless food particles and commensal bacteria. And they form a protective barrier against disease-causing organisms by competing for nutrients and attachment sites on the intestinal wall.

The composition of the gut microbiome is shaped by numerous factors, including genetics, mode of birth delivery, breastfeeding, diet, antibiotic use, age, and geographic location. Babies born by Caesarean section acquire a different initial microbiome — dominated by skin and hospital-environment bacteria — compared to those delivered vaginally, who are colonised by their mother's vaginal and intestinal bacteria. Some researchers have suggested that the rising rates of Caesarean deliveries in developed countries may contribute to increased rates of allergies, asthma, and autoimmune conditions, though the evidence remains inconclusive. Diet has perhaps the most significant and modifiable effect on microbiome composition. A diet rich in diverse plant-based foods promotes a diverse and stable microbiome, while a diet high in processed foods and sugar tends to reduce microbial diversity and promote inflammation-associated bacteria.

The gut-brain axis — the bidirectional communication pathway between the gut microbiome and the brain — has emerged as one of the most exciting areas of microbiome research. Studies in mice have shown that germ-free animals raised without any microorganisms display altered behaviour, including increased anxiety-like responses and reduced social interaction. Remarkably, transplanting gut bacteria from bold, exploratory mice into anxious mice can change their behaviour, suggesting that gut microbes directly influence brain function and mood. In humans, research has linked alterations in the gut microbiome to conditions including depression, anxiety, autism spectrum disorder, and Parkinson's disease. A 2019 study published in Nature Microbiology found that people with depression consistently had lower levels of two specific groups of bacteria — Coprococcus and Dialister — regardless of whether they were taking antidepressant medication.

The therapeutic potential of the microbiome is beginning to be realised. Faecal microbiota transplantation, in which stool from a healthy donor is introduced into the gut of a patient, has proven remarkably effective against recurrent Clostridioides difficile infection, achieving cure rates of over 90 percent — far superior to antibiotics. Clinical trials are exploring FMT as a treatment for inflammatory bowel disease, obesity, metabolic syndrome, and even certain cancers. Meanwhile, the probiotics industry — encompassing supplements, functional foods, and beverages containing live beneficial bacteria — has grown into a market worth over 60 billion dollars globally. However, many scientists caution that the evidence for most commercial probiotic products remains limited, and that the field is still far from being able to prescribe specific microbial interventions for individual patients. The future of microbiome medicine will likely involve precision approaches — tailoring microbial therapies to an individual's unique microbiome profile and health needs — but achieving this vision will require much deeper understanding of the complex interactions between the thousands of microbial species that call the human body home.

prompt.en: Some people believe that children should be taught to be competitive. Others argue that children should learn to cooperate rather than compete. Discuss both views and give your own opinion. Give reasons for your answer and include any relevant examples from your own knowledge or experience. Write at least 250 words.
prompt.zh: 一些人认为应该教孩子具有竞争意识。另一些人则认为孩子应该学会合作而不是竞争。讨论两种观点并给出你自己的意见。给出你回答的理由，并包括你自己的知识或经验中任何相关的例子。至少写250个单词。
